newsitem.title: USA: USDA criticized for slowness on racial complaints.
newsitem.headline: USDA criticized for slowness on racial complaints.

text.p: The head of the U.S. Agriculture Department took two senior officials "to the woodshed" and insisted they work together to resolve hundreds of complaints of racial discrimination by the agency, a top deputy of Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Thursday.

Glickman himself came in for some mild scolding from the House Agriculture committee during a lengthy hearing on the agency's progress in clearing the backlog of complaints from black farmers and minority employees.
Last February, the USDA launched a programme to combat racial bias throughout the agency, including a federal take-over of 12,000 county employees who run local offices.

But efforts to resolve the more than 700 complaints filed with the agency have been hampered by squabbling between USDA's office of general counsel and the agency's fledgling civil rights unit, according to Representative Benny Thompson, D-Miss.
Glickman has privately insisted that intra-agency bickering end, said Pearlie Reed, acting assistant secretary for administration at USDA.
"We both were taken to the woodshed by the secretary," Reed said, referring to his counterpart who heads the USDA's office of general counsel.

Representative Maxine Waters, D-Calif., testified that despite negotiations by Reed and his colleagues to reach a settlement in some cases, the agency's lawyers vetoed the efforts saying the USDA lacked legal authority to settle cases that did not make a specific finding of discrimination.
Waters asked the House panel to order an investigation of USDA by the Justice Department.

Glickman acknowledged that the USDA has a "disgraceful" record of resolving complaints of racial discrimination over the years but is now hiring investigators that should allow it to clear the backlog of cases within a year.
The agency's investigative division was closed by the Reagan Administration in the early 1980s.
Many of the complaints were filed by black farmers, who contend they were treated unfairly or denied federal government programme assistance by USDA employees in field offices around the nation.
Other cases were filed by USDA employees claiming they were not given the same opportunities as white employees.
